problem: This paper examines whether hardware noise places a fundamental limit on variational quantum algorithms.
gap: Earlier barren plateau work linked vanishing gradients to random parameter initialisation in noise-free circuits, leaving the effect of noise itself unsettled.
method: The authors give a rigorous proof for local Pauli noise, covering a generic ansatz that includes alternating operator and unitary coupled cluster circuits. Numerical work with a realistic hardware noise model supports it.
results: When circuit depth grows linearly with qubit number, gradients shrink exponentially with qubit count. These noise-induced plateaus differ in concept from the noise-free kind.
limits: The proof assumes a particular noise model and depth scaling. It warns against deep circuits but does not by itself show how much shallow, small circuits are affected.
mm: Proof under local Pauli noise; numerics with hardware noise model
f: Gradients vanish exponentially when depth grows linearly with qubits
l: Assumes specific noise and depth scaling

problem: This paper explores the relationship between how expressive an ansatz is and how large its gradients are.
gap: Barren plateau results were known for ansatze forming exact 2-designs, but not for arbitrary circuits used in practice.
method: The authors extend the analysis to general ansatze, calculating gradient variance in terms of the distance of the ansatz from a 2-design, and they provide numerical illustrations.
results: The bounds indicate that highly expressive ansatze have flatter cost landscapes and are harder to train. Expressibility therefore comes at a cost, and this must be considered when designing circuits that avoid plateaus.
limits: The analysis concerns gradient behaviour and does not identify the best ansatz for a particular dataset. Less expressive circuits may also be unable to represent the required solution.
f: Highly expressive ansatze give flatter landscapes, harder to train
l: Does not select an ansatz for a given dataset

problem: This foundational paper applies transfer learning to networks that combine classical and quantum parts.
gap: Intermediate-scale quantum devices cannot process high-dimensional data such as images directly.
method: Several hybrid schemes are proposed, mainly a pre-trained classical network followed by a final variational quantum circuit. Proof-of-concept examples cover image recognition and quantum state classification, with PennyLane experiments on IBM and Rigetti computers.
results: The classical part can pre-process large inputs and pass a small set of informative features to the quantum processor, and a high-resolution image classifier was tested on two real quantum computers.
limits: These are proofs of concept, and the classical network carries much of the feature extraction, so the specific contribution of the quantum layer needs separate evaluation.
mm: Pre-trained network plus VQC; IBM and Rigetti tests
f: Classical pre-processing makes large inputs feasible on small devices
l: Proof of concept; quantum contribution unclear

problem: This paper designs a quantum-classical analogue of a convolutional neural network that suits current noisy devices.
gap: Deep learning recognises patterns well, and quantum circuits can produce distributions that are hard to generate classically, yet the two needed a practical bridge that respects limited qubits and depth.
method: The authors propose a hybrid network that uses quantum circuits to enhance feature mapping, with a framework that computes gradients of hybrid loss functions automatically. It was tested on a Tetris dataset.
results: The hybrid network exceeded the learning accuracy of a classical CNN with the same structure while keeping nonlinearity and scalability.
limits: The Tetris dataset is simple and the classical comparison used the same structure only, so a stronger tuned baseline might narrow the reported gap.
mm: Quantum feature mapping; automatic gradients; Tetris data
f: Higher learning accuracy than same-structure CNN

problem: This study benchmarks fully parameterised quantum convolutional neural networks on classical data.
gap: Many quantum analogues of the CNN had been proposed, but how design choices affect classical data classification needed systematic comparison.
method: Using only two-qubit interactions, the authors varied circuit structures, data encoding, classical pre-processing, cost functions and optimisers on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST.
results: Accuracy was excellent in most cases despite few free parameters, and the quantum networks performed noticeably better than CNNs under similar training conditions. Their shallow circuits suit near-term devices.
limits: The result compares models trained under similar conditions, which may favour small models, and the datasets are image benchmarks. Results may differ for tabular medical features or under real device noise.
mm: Design comparison on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST
f: High accuracy with few parameters; better than CNNs under similar conditions
l: Image benchmarks; comparison depends on training conditions

problem: This paper asks how far variational classifiers and quantum kernel SVMs can, in principle, extend quantum advantage.
gap: The search for advantage in QML models needed a precise theoretical statement of what these model types can solve.
method: The authors construct a classification problem from the k-Forrelation problem, which is PromiseBQP-complete, and show that both model types can solve it.
results: A suitable feature map and quantum kernel exist that make these models efficient solvers for any BQP problem. They can therefore be designed for an advantage on classification problems that are quantum-tractable but classically intractable.
limits: This is an existence result about designed feature maps. It gives no route to finding one for natural data, and it reports no performance on practical datasets.
technique: Complexity theory of VQC and QSVM
f: Suitable feature maps can solve any BQP problem
l: Existence result; no practical feature map or data

problem: This experiment tests whether quantum classifiers are vulnerable to small, deliberately crafted changes in their input.
gap: Theory predicted this weakness, which matters in safety-critical settings, but it had not been demonstrated experimentally.
method: The authors trained variational classifiers on ten transmon qubits, with average two-qubit gate fidelity above 99.4%, using real images including medical MRI scans as well as quantum data.
results: Classifiers reaching test accuracy up to 99% were deceived by small adversarial perturbations, and adversarial training substantially improved their robustness.
limits: The work addresses security, not whether quantum classifiers outperform classical ones. Protection was shown against the perturbations studied, and wider clinical robustness remains open.
mm: Ten superconducting qubits; images, MRI and quantum data
f: Up to 99% accuracy, yet small perturbations deceive; adversarial training helps
l: Security focus; wider clinical robustness open

problem: This study assesses whether QML is feasible on real clinical datasets using actual hardware.
gap: Progress in QML had not been matched by broad testing on open clinical data with near-term devices.
method: The authors propose a quantum distance classifier and a simplified quantum-kernel SVM. Data was embedded with logarithmic encoding and run on the 15-qubit IBMQ Melbourne computer, then compared with earlier QML and classical methods on three open clinical datasets.
results: The distance classifier did better on datasets with few samples and features, and kernel methods did better on larger ones. The encoding raised the area under the ROC curve by up to 2%.
limits: The abstract reports relative comparisons rather than a clear win over classical models, and the 2% gain is small and specific to the tested datasets.
technique: Quantum distance classifier; simplified quantum-kernel SVM
mm: IBMQ Melbourne, 15 qubits, three open clinical datasets
f: Best method depends on data size; encoding adds up to 2% AUC
l: No clear win over classical; small gain

problem: This work classifies full-image mammograms from the BCDR collection as malignant or benign with a hybrid quantum model.
gap: The authors wanted to learn whether the transfer learning idea of Mari et al. could benefit a hard medical imaging task.
method: They trained a set of hybrid classical-quantum networks with transfer learning, used heatmaps to inspect the image regions targeted, evaluated several metrics, and also ran experiments on a real quantum device.
results: Accuracy reached 84%, against 76.9% for the state-of-the-art work they compared with. Some architectures suited particular tasks better, and the method may help generalisation on complex data.
limits: The authors themselves state that further tests are needed. Much of the feature extraction is classical, so the gain cannot be credited to the quantum part alone.
mm: Mammograms from BCDR; simulator and real device
l: Further tests needed; quantum share of the gain unclear

problem: This paper applies a quantum SVM to the binary diagnosis of malignant breast cancer.
gap: The authors aim to improve on using a quantum SVM alone by also optimising its parameters against several objectives.
method: The quantum SVM is combined with an elitist non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm that tunes its parameters, and quantum kernel estimation is run in an IBM QSVM simulator.
results: The authors report remarkably accurate results compared with a classical SVM and an execution time of 0.14, although the abstract states neither a specific accuracy figure nor a unit for that time.
limits: Without those figures in the abstract, the size of the claimed gain cannot be judged from it. Execution on a simulator also leaves real hardware noise unexamined.
mm: Breast cancer diagnosis; IBM QSVM simulator
f: Authors report high accuracy against classical SVM
l: Abstract gives no accuracy figure; simulator only
